q: In Grade 10, one dimensional motion such as linear motion and free fall motion was studied.
e: This is a direct statement from the textbook introducing the progression from one-dimensional to two-dimensional motion.

q: Two-dimensional motion is the simplest type of motion which can be encountered in many cases.
e: One dimensional motion, not two-dimensional motion, is the simplest type of motion.

q: In two-dimensional motion, the object may move in both the x and y direction simultaneously.
e: Two-dimensional motion involves simultaneous movement in both the x and y directions.

q: In order to describe the motion of an object in two dimensions, scalar concept must be used.
e: Vector concept, not scalar concept, must be used to describe two-dimensional motion.

q: The displacement vector of the object from P to Q is $\Delta \vec{r}$.
e: The displacement vector representing the change in position from point P to Q is denoted as $\Delta \vec{r}$.

q: The perpendicular components of $\Delta \vec{r}$ are $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$.
e: The displacement vector $\Delta \vec{r}$ can be resolved into perpendicular x and y components, $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$.

q: The magnitude of $\Delta \vec{r}$ is given by $\Delta r = \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 - (\Delta y)^2}$.
e: The magnitude is given by the Pythagorean theorem: $\Delta r = \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2}$.

q: To find the direction of $\Delta \vec{r}$, the formula $\tan \theta = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ is used.
e: The angle $\theta$ of the displacement vector is determined using the ratio of its y-component to its x-component.

q: Instantaneous velocity is given by $\vec{v} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}$.
e: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of the average velocity as the time interval approaches zero.

q: Average acceleration is given by $\vec{a}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}$.
e: Average acceleration is defined as the change in velocity divided by the time taken.

q: Instantaneous acceleration is given by $\vec{a} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}$.
e: Instantaneous acceleration is the limit of average acceleration as the time interval approaches zero.

q: An object moving with constant speed along a curved path is not accelerating.
e: An object moving with constant speed along a curved path is accelerating because the direction of its velocity is changing.

q: The direction of the velocity of an object moving along a curved path is tangential to its path.
e: At any point on a curved path, the velocity vector is directed tangentially to the path.

q: An object is accelerated whenever the velocity changes in magnitude, direction, or both.
e: Acceleration occurs with any change in the velocity vector, whether in magnitude, direction, or both.

q: A projectile is any object thrown into space upon which the only acting force is the gravity.
e: By definition, a projectile is an object acted upon solely by gravity after being thrown into space.

q: The path followed by a projectile is known as a displacement.
e: The path followed by a projectile is known as a trajectory.

q: The motion of an object moving in both horizontal x direction and vertical y direction simultaneously is called the projectile motion.
e: Projectile motion is characterized by simultaneous motion in both horizontal and vertical directions.

q: If air resistance is neglected, an object moves along the horizontal x direction with a constant acceleration.
e: If air resistance is neglected, an object moves along the horizontal x direction with a constant velocity, not acceleration.

q: If air resistance is neglected, an object moves in the vertical y direction with constant downward acceleration.
e: In the vertical direction, the object experiences a constant downward acceleration due to gravity.

q: In projectile motion with neglected air resistance, only gravitational force is acting on the object.
e: Gravity is the sole force acting on a projectile when air resistance is ignored.

q: The downward acceleration is the acceleration due to gravity $g$ which is a constant over the range of motion.
e: The acceleration due to gravity $g$ is treated as a constant throughout the projectile's range.

q: The vertical motion of a projectile is a uniform motion.
e: The vertical motion of a projectile is a free fall motion, not a uniform motion.

q: In the x direction of projectile motion, $a_x = 0$ and $v_x = v_0 \cos \theta = \text{constant}$.
e: There is no horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal velocity component remains constant.

q: The horizontal displacement of a projectile can be written as a function of time as $x = (v_0 \cos \theta) t$.
e: Since horizontal velocity is constant, horizontal displacement is simply velocity multiplied by time.

q: In the y direction of projectile motion, $v_{oy}$ is the initial velocity and $a_y$ is $-g$.
e: The initial vertical velocity is $v_{oy}$ and the acceleration is downward, hence $-g$.

q: The velocity of a projectile in the y direction in time $t$ is given by $v_y = v_{oy} + gt$.
e: The correct equation is $v_y = v_{oy} - gt$ because the acceleration due to gravity acts downward.

q: The displacement of a projectile in the y direction in time $t$ is given by $y = v_{oy} t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
e: This is the standard kinematic equation for vertical displacement under constant downward acceleration.

q: The magnitude of the velocity of the projectile at any instant of time is $v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$.
e: The total velocity magnitude is found using the Pythagorean theorem on its perpendicular components.

q: The direction of the velocity of the projectile is given by $\tan \theta = \frac{v_x}{v_y}$.
e: The direction is given by $\tan \theta = \frac{v_y}{v_x}$, the ratio of the vertical component to the horizontal component.

q: The projectile reaches the highest point when its horizontal component of velocity $v_x$ is zero.
e: The projectile reaches the highest point when its vertical component of velocity $v_y$ is zero.

q: The time taken to reach the highest point is $t_1 = \frac{v_0 \sin \theta}{g}$.
e: This is derived by setting the final vertical velocity $v_y$ to zero in the velocity-time equation.

q: The time of flight is equal to the time to reach the maximum height.
e: The time of flight is twice the time to reach the maximum height.

q: The time of flight of a projectile is $T = \frac{2 v_0 \sin \theta}{g}$.
e: The total time of flight is double the time taken to reach the peak of the trajectory.

q: The maximum height of the projectile is $H = \frac{(v_0 \cos \theta)^2}{2g}$.
e: The maximum height depends on the vertical component of velocity: $H = \frac{(v_0 \sin \theta)^2}{2g}$.

q: The horizontal range $R$ is the horizontal distance from the starting point to the point where the projectile returns to the same height.
e: This is the exact definition of horizontal range in projectile motion.

q: The horizontal range is obtained as $R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$.
e: This formula is derived by substituting the time of flight into the horizontal displacement equation.

q: For an object thrown horizontally, there is a vertical component to its initial velocity.
e: For an object thrown horizontally, there is no vertical component to its initial velocity ($v_{oy} = 0$).

q: For an object thrown horizontally, the vertical velocity of the object in time $t$ is $v_y = -gt$.
e: Since initial vertical velocity is zero, the vertical velocity at time $t$ is solely due to gravitational acceleration.

q: For an object thrown horizontally, the vertical displacement in time $t$ is $y = -\frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
e: With zero initial vertical velocity, the vertical displacement follows the free fall equation.

q: Circular motion is a specific type of a two-dimensional motion.
e: Circular motion occurs in a plane, making it a specific type of two-dimensional motion.

q: Circular motion is a movement of an object along the circumference of a circle or rotation along a circular path.
e: This is the textbook definition of circular motion.

q: Although an object moves in a circle at a constant speed, its velocity is constant.
e: Although the speed is constant, the velocity is not constant because its direction is continuously changing.

q: In circular motion, the direction of the velocity is tangential to the path.
e: The velocity vector at any point in circular motion is directed along the tangent to the circle at that point.

q: Velocity is constantly changing in circular motion because the direction of the velocity is changing continuously.
e: A change in direction constitutes a change in velocity, even if the speed remains constant.

q: The velocity in circular motion is also called the tangential velocity.
e: Because the velocity vector is always tangent to the circular path, it is referred to as tangential velocity.

q: Change of the angular position is called the angular displacement $\theta$.
e: Angular displacement represents the change in the angular position of an object.

q: The angular displacement is the ratio of the radius to the arc length.
e: The angular displacement is the ratio of the arc length to the radius ($\theta = \frac{s}{r}$).

q: The magnitude of angular displacement $\theta$, measured in radian (rad), is given by $\theta = \frac{s}{r}$.
e: This is the fundamental definition of angular displacement in radians.

q: One radian is defined as the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius of the circle.
e: This is the exact geometric definition of one radian.

q: One revolution is equal to $360^{\circ}$ or $\pi \text{ rad}$.
e: One revolution is equal to $360^{\circ}$ or $2\pi \text{ rad}$.

q: Average angular velocity is the ratio of the change in angular displacement to time taken.
e: Average angular velocity measures how much angular displacement occurs per unit of time.

q: Average angular velocity is given by $\omega_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t}$.
e: This is the mathematical representation of the definition of average angular velocity.

q: Instantaneous angular velocity is defined as the time rate of change of angular displacement.
e: Instantaneous angular velocity is the derivative of angular displacement with respect to time.

q: Instantaneous angular velocity can be written as $\omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt}$.
e: This is the calculus definition of instantaneous angular velocity.

q: Angular velocity is measured in radian per second ($\text{rad s}^{-1}$), revolution per second (rps), and revolution per minute (rpm).
e: These are the standard units for measuring angular velocity as stated in the text.

q: The average angular acceleration is the ratio of change of angular velocity to time taken.
e: Average angular acceleration measures the rate of change of angular velocity over a time interval.

q: Average angular acceleration is given by $\alpha_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \omega}{\Delta t}$.
e: This is the mathematical formula for average angular acceleration.

q: Instantaneous angular acceleration is the time rate of change of angular velocity.
e: Instantaneous angular acceleration is the derivative of angular velocity with respect to time.

q: Instantaneous angular acceleration can be defined as $\alpha = \frac{d\omega}{dt}$.
e: This is the calculus definition of instantaneous angular acceleration.

q: When a body is moving with a constant angular acceleration $\alpha$, it is given by $\alpha = \frac{\omega - \omega_0}{t}$.
e: This is the rearranged kinematic equation for constant angular acceleration.

q: Angular acceleration is measured in radian per second ($\text{rad s}^{-1}$).
e: Angular acceleration is measured in radian per second squared ($\text{rad s}^{-2}$).

q: The magnitude of the angular velocity is related to that of the tangential velocity as $v = \frac{\omega}{r}$.
e: The correct relationship is $v = r\omega$, where tangential velocity equals radius times angular velocity.

q: The relation between the angular acceleration $\alpha$ and the tangential acceleration $a$ is $a = r\alpha$.
e: Tangential acceleration is the product of the radius and the angular acceleration.

q: Angular velocity $\omega$ and angular acceleration $\alpha$ are scalar quantities.
e: Angular velocity $\omega$ and angular acceleration $\alpha$ are vector quantities.

q: The direction of linear acceleration $a$ is tangential to the path, and it is called the tangential acceleration.
e: The component of linear acceleration that is tangent to the circular path is specifically called tangential acceleration.
